newsitem.title: USA: Secondhand smoke more dangerous on jets, researcher says.
newsitem.headline: Secondhand smoke more dangerous on jets, researcher says.

text.p: The former head of the federal government's main cigarette-research group testified in a landmark anti-tobacco trial Thursday that secondhand cigarette smoke on American passenger jets was more dangerous than in the home.

"I would say the exposure in airplanes is much more intensive, much more serious, much more dangerous than the exposure in homes," testified Ronald Davis, head of the U.S. Office of Smoking and Health from 1987 to 1991.

Davis told the six jurors hearing the $5 billion lawsuit brought by non-smoking flight attendants with lung cancer and other diseases that secondhand cigarette smoke contained 4,000 to 5,000 chemicals and constituted a health danger to anyone routinely taking in smoke from other people's cigarettes.
"It was definitely a cause of lung cancer in flight attendants who are exposed over a period of time to tobacco smoke," Davis said.
Smoking aboard U.S. airliners was banned in 1988. The seven tobacco companies and two trade groups fighting the lawsuit deny secondhand smoke caused the flight attendants' injuries.

Davis said during questioning by plaintiffs' lawyer Stanley Rosenblatt that the smoke arising from burning cigarettes is even more heavily packed with many cancer-causing chemicals than the fumes inhaled by smokers.
Cigarette smoke contains lead, formaldehyde and benzene, among many other cancer-causing chemicals, said Davis, a physician and expert in the causes of diseases among large groups of people.
"Some of these elements are in higher concentration in the smoke that comes off the cigarette than the smoke the smoker takes in," Davis said.

Davis said modern aircraft were especially risky for secondhand-smoke exposure because as many as 50 to 60 passengers might be smoking and that the ventilation systems aboard jets did not allow for fresh air.
"On an airplane, you can't open a window," Davis said.

The lawyers fighting the lawsuit, Norma Broin et al vs. Philip Morris Inc et al, claim the average flight attendant spent only about 12 hours a week in closed cabins during the late 1980s and that the rate of lung cancer and other diseases linked to smoke among non-smoking flight attendants was the same as among other non-smokers.

During cross-examination by Jeffrey Furr, an attorney for RJ Reynolds Tobacco Co., Davis said the annual reports on smoking issued by the U.S. surgeon general have yet to label secondhand smoke as a sure cause of disease among non-smokers.
Davis oversaw the preparations of three surgeon general reports during his years a head of the Office of Smoking and Health.

Testimony in the case on behalf of an estimated 60,000 flight attendants was expected to last through at least September. It is both the first secondhand-smoke case and the first class-action lawsuit against the U.S. tobacco industry to come to trial.
